summary: Defines how an ALTO client can discover ALTO servers when the information about network topology is partitioned across domains. ALTO gives applications guidance for choosing among candidate hosts, but a client first has to find a server that can provide it.

plainLanguage.summary: Before asking for travel advice, you need to know whom to ask. This explains how a program finds the right advice-giving server.

questions: how does alto find a server using dns
what is a u-naptr record for alto
subtitle: How an ALTO client uses reverse DNS to find the server that knows about a particular IP address or prefix.

tldr.problem: ALTO servers may each know only part of the network. A client that wants guidance about a specific IP address needs a way to find the server that can actually answer, even if it lives in another domain.
tldr.mechanism: The client takes an IP address or prefix and a U-NAPTR service parameter (usually "ALTO:https"), turns the address into a reverse DNS name, and looks up NAPTR records there, trying shorter prefixes until one lookup succeeds. The records give the URIs of ALTO servers.
tldr.outcome: A client can find a competent ALTO server for any address whose reverse DNS carries the right records. The security story depends on DNSSEC, because forged records would send clients to the wrong server.

today: RFC 8686 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Cross-Domain Discovery
sections.content:
Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) gives applications guidance for choosing among candidate hosts that could provide a resource. The base protocol, RFC 7285, defines how a client talks to one server and assumes that server can answer any query, perhaps with a default value when it has no exact data.

That assumption breaks when knowledge is partitioned. Some servers have accurate information about one part of the network and others about another part. A topologically nearby server, such as one found with the procedure in RFC 7286, may then not help. This matters most when the ALTO client is not an endpoint of the transfer being optimized, for example a tracker in a peer-to-peer application (the RFC works through such a case in an appendix).

RFC 8686 specifies the ALTO Cross-Domain Server Discovery Procedure. A client calls it with one IP address or prefix and gets back URIs of servers that can give a competent answer for that address. The people who control the reverse DNS for a prefix, typically an ISP, a corporate IT department or a university, publish the records. They may point to their own ALTO server or to someone else's, such as an upstream ISP.
sections.plainLanguage: Some advice-givers only know about their own part of town. If you want advice about a faraway street, you need to find the expert for that street first. This document is how you find them.

sections.title: The Idea in Brief
sections.content:
The procedure builds on the DNS trees in-addr.arpa. and ip6.arpa., which are normally used for reverse mapping of addresses to names with PTR records. Here they hold U-NAPTR records (RFC 4848), which map a domain name to URIs. The design was inspired by LIS discovery using reverse DNS (RFC 7216) and reuses parts of the basic ALTO server discovery.

The call takes two parameters: X, an IPv4 or IPv6 address or prefix in CIDR notation, and SP, a U-NAPTR service parameter. SP is usually ALTO:https, but values such as ALTO:http (for unencrypted debugging) may be used, and the procedure MUST accept any valid service parameter. The result is a list of URIs, usually of ALTO Information Resource Directories (IRDs), with order and preference values to consider when there are several.

Two lookup strategies are tried in sequence. First the most specific name is looked up. If that gives nothing usable, names for shorter prefixes are tried. This supports both per-address deployments and large deployments that cover many addresses with few DNS records.
sections.plainLanguage: You look up the exact house first. If nobody there has left a note, you check the street, then the neighbourhood, until you find a note saying who to ask.

sections.title: Building the Reverse DNS Names
sections.content:
Step 1 checks the prefix length L. If the address is IPv4 and L is below 8, or IPv6 and L is below 32, the procedure aborts with an "unsupported prefix length" error. Otherwise it builds the full reverse name: R32 for IPv4 under IN-ADDR.ARPA. (rules from RFC 1035) or R128 for IPv6 under IP6.ARPA. (rules from RFC 3596). For example, 198.51.100.3 gives 3.100.51.198.IN-ADDR.ARPA..

Step 2 builds shorter names with an auxiliary function skip(str,n), which drops everything up to and including the n-th dot. For IPv4 this yields R24, R16 and R8; dropping one label shortens the prefix by 8 bits. For IPv6 it yields R64, R56, R48, R40 and R32; dropping one hex digit shortens the prefix by 4 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: An address is written backwards to make a lookup name, like reading a postal address from the house number outward. Cutting off pieces from the front gives you the names of the bigger areas around it.

sections.title: The U-NAPTR Lookups
sections.content:
Step 3 uses a table to pick the first name to look up based on the address type and the prefix length. For an IPv4 /32, the first lookup (which the procedure MUST do) is R32, and the procedure SHOULD then try R24, R16 and R8 in that order. A /24 to /31 starts at R24, and so on. The chosen name plus the service parameter is used for a U-NAPTR lookup (RFC 4848) to obtain URIs for the server's IRD.

The RFC gives an example in which two NAPTR records at 100.51.198.IN-ADDR.ARPA. point to https://alto1.example.net/ird and https://alto2.example.net/ird, with the first preferred (preference values 10 and 20, with the same order value 100). If a lookup finds records, the procedure returns them and ends successfully. If no name from either column yields an IRD URI, it ends unsuccessfully and returns an empty URI list.
sections.plainLanguage: The lookup starts at the most exact name and walks outward. The first place that has a note with a server address wins, and if no place has one, you get an empty answer.

sections.title: Errors and Retries
sections.content:
Invalid parameters or an unsupported prefix length abort the procedure and the error is reported to the caller. Individual DNS lookups can fail in three ways: a normal condition (the name exists but has no ALTO NAPTR records), a permanent error (the name does not exist) or a temporary error (such as a timeout). In all three cases the procedure SHOULD immediately try the next name. Only after all names have been tried MAY it retry the ones that failed temporarily.

The reasoning is that ALTO is advisory: applications should not depend on it for basic function, so a quick answer, even a less accurate one, or a quick conclusion that no server exists, is preferable to long delays. If temporary DNS errors occurred, the procedure SHOULD tell its caller so that a later retry might do better.
sections.plainLanguage: If one phone book page is torn out, you just move on to the next page instead of waiting. At the end you can say, "some pages were missing, so maybe try again later."

sections.title: Using It with ALTO Services and in Deployments
sections.content:
The procedure works best with the Endpoint Property Service and the Endpoint Cost Service, which both take IP addresses. For the Endpoint Cost Service the RFC distinguishes cases. With one source and many destinations, the client calls the procedure once with the source address; with many sources and one destination, once with the destination. Using a single call keeps all queries on one server so results are comparable, which matters for metrics like routingcost that have no well-defined base unit. With many of both, the client should split the work by source (or alternatively by destination). It is less useful for fetching full network and cost maps, since the cost map reached this way may be very sparse.

For clients, the RFC discusses discovery with the client's own address (which may require STUN to learn the public address behind a NAT), dual-stack and multihomed hosts that may use different source addresses, and mobile hosts, which SHOULD query the resource directory again after an address change. A resource directory behind the same NAT as a consumer sees a private address, and the RFC says using that address may be problematic.

For operators, one invocation can cause up to six NAPTR lookups for IPv6 and up to four for IPv4. Publishing records for individual addresses or long prefixes ends the search early, and a longer TTL for negative answers also reduces load. An operator with an IPv4 /18 could install 64 records (one per /24) or team up with neighbours and run one shared ALTO server with a single record. The procedure is compatible with classless reverse delegation (BCP 20, RFC 2317), and an ISP that does not delegate reverse DNS to customers can publish records at the /24 name on their behalf.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask about many routes at once, you should ask one expert so the answers can be compared fairly. And the people who run the phone book can keep lookups short by putting notes at the most useful places.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The most serious concern is integrity of the server URI. An attacker who can modify or spoof DNS records could send clients to a wrong server, which might give no guidance, give poor or forged information, try to shift traffic or hurt application performance, or threaten user privacy. The mitigation is DNSSEC (RFC 4033): all implementations MUST support DNSSEC or use it from the operating system, and operators publishing U-NAPTR records SHOULD sign their in-addr.arpa. and ip6.arpa. subdomains. The later HTTPS certificate check cannot detect forged discovery records, so those records have to be secured by DNSSEC themselves.

For availability, if discovery is blocked, applications run without ALTO guidance and behave as in a deployment without ALTO; operators should follow best practice to protect DNS and ALTO servers against denial of service. The server URI is treated as public, so no confidentiality protection is provided. For client privacy, an eavesdropper could learn that a client is using ALTO for an address; DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) and DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484) can protect these queries between the client and its recursive servers.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone swaps the address in the phone book, you might visit a fake expert. A tamper-proof seal on the book, called DNSSEC, lets you notice the swap.
